item.title: Burnham Hopes for ‘Common Ground’ With Trump in First Meeting
item.description:
On Jan. 6, 2021, as rioters assaulted the U.S. Capitol to try to stop the certification of President Trump’s re-election loss, Andy Burnham, the Labour mayor of Greater Manchester, England, posted some words on social media.

“Any UK politician who gave Trump the time of day should be ashamed right now,” Mr. Burnham, now Britain’s prime minister, wrote that day.

On Tuesday, Mr. Burnham will give Mr. Trump more than a little of his own time as the two men sit down together, face-to-face, for the first time. The two have talked twice on the phone, but the meeting in New York will be the British prime minister’s most high-profile — and high-stakes — meeting with another world leader since he took office this summer.

“We’ve found a connection,” Mr. Burnham told reporters as he flew to New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly. “So, I will go with where I feel it’s right, to meet him where he is at, and search for that common ground, which I’m sure we’ll find.”

“I’m looking forward to it,” he added.

Earlier this summer, when Mr. Burnham was asked about how he would deal with Mr. Trump, he said, “I sense it’ll be a bit of a challenge.”

In the near term, that challenge involves finding a way to avoid kindling Mr. Trump’s ire on issues such as drilling for oil in the North Sea or refusing to participate more aggressively in the U.S. war on Iran. Mr. Trump has already lashed out at Britain on both issues, and Mr. Burnham will most likely want to avoid antagonizing him further.

On the plane to New York on Monday night, Mr. Burnham said he wanted to focus the conversation with Mr. Trump on three things: closer cooperation on AI; efforts to bring about a peaceful and just resolution in Ukraine; and a discussion about how to end the conflict in the Middle East, which has had deep impacts on the price of energy, food and other goods in Britain.

Over the long run, Mr. Burnham will be looking to navigate a rapidly changing relationship with Washington in which Britain aims to become less reliant on the United States for trade and security. Mr. Trump has made it clear that he no longer believes in the “special relationship” that served as a bond between the two countries since World War II.

Last year, the president referred to Britain as “our once Great Ally” in a social media post, saying he was angry with Keir Starmer, then the prime minister, for refusing to help attack Iran. “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” the president wrote.

During his time in office, Mr. Starmer expended a lot of effort trying to placate Mr. Trump. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said in an interview with The New York Times this summer that Mr. Burnham should not follow his predecessor’s approach.

“The thing about a special relationship is that it’s akin to having a best friend,” Mr. Khan said. “When you’ve got a best friend you expect more from them to a casual acquaintance or a work colleague and that means saying boo to a goose, calling them out when they’re wrong.”

“I think we know there are some people who have been sycophantic to President Trump — it’s not worked out too well for them,” Mr. Khan added. “So Andy should be true to himself.”

Mr. Burnham’s advisers have said that they expect the British prime minister to take a more cautious approach with Mr. Trump than Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada or Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of Spain have done in recent months. After trade talks with the United States collapsed this month, Mr. Carney declared that Canada was “at war” with America, adding, “You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked.”

But Mr. Burnham’s aides say that he will not shrink from making announcements that Mr. Trump may dislike. Mr. Burnham is expected to announce in the coming weeks whether he will approve two oil and gas projects in the North Sea. While he has signaled that he will take a more “pragmatic” approach to drilling, possibly by approving one or both fields, Mr. Burnham has also pledged to stick to Labour’s election promise not to issue new drilling licenses.

That could lead the prime minister to a decision that is not as expansive as Mr. Trump might hope.

Shortly after Mr. Burnham was chosen to lead the Labour Party and become prime minister, Mr. Trump said, “I hear he’s extremely liberal, extremely. So that means he probably won’t open up the North Sea.” But following a telephone conversation several weeks later, Mr. Trump said: “He said he’s going to open up North Sea oil. If he does that, you’re going to be a wealthy country.”

Stephen Castle contributed reporting from London.

item.title: Cold War Lessons for A.I.
item.description:
The potential dangers of A.I. are weighing on many minds this week. They’re being discussed by world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly; they will almost certainly be discussed when Donald Trump and Xi Jinping sit down for talks tomorrow in Washington.

Calls for global cooperation to slow the development of what is known as frontier A.I. — the most advanced, most capable A.I. models — have grown louder. So far there isn’t a whole lot of optimism about the world’s two A.I. superpowers reaching an agreement any time soon.

But there’s a precedent for this moment. Today, I write about what global efforts to control nuclear weapons can teach us about controlling A.I.

Two rival superpowers. Technology that has the capacity to be enormously destructive. A moment of awakening that reveals just how much danger the world could be in.

There’s a lot that’s unprecedented about this moment when it comes to A.I. But in some respects, we’ve been here before.

During the Cold War, the U.S. and the Soviet Union were sworn enemies, locked in a race to build ever more, and ever more powerful, nuclear weapons. Then came the Cuban Missile Crisis. Thirteen tense days focused minds, and in the years that followed, the two nations went on to contain what was then the gravest known threat to humanity.

It’s easy to forget that a lot of people didn’t think this was possible. Today, commentators and officials are skeptical about an A.I. treaty between the U.S. and China, too.

The nuclear analogy goes only so far. There are important differences between artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons, and some of those might make reaching an agreement to constrain A.I. more difficult. But some could arguably make it easier.

Vast differences

Artificial intelligence and nuclear weapons are very different technologies.

They’re used differently. A.I. is developed by private companies, and is effectively in the hands of anyone who has access to a computer or smartphone. Nuclear weapons are … not. They’re controlled by governments. Even their civilian equivalent, nuclear power plants, require expensive, highly specialized physical infrastructure. (Though the differences are not as stark as they might seem — more on that in a bit.)

But perhaps the biggest difference is that nuclear technology was well understood for decades before the world moved to control the spread of nuclear weapons.

A.I., by contrast, remains something of a black box. Even America’s frontier labs cannot always understand their own A.I. models; indeed, that is one of the worries driving calls to slow down the technology. But it’s not easy to regulate something you don’t understand.

Trust but verify 2.0

Still, some principles of nuclear arms control can be applied directly to A.I. For instance, the first step toward any agreement between two deeply distrustful parties is to build, well, trust. And the way to do that is to start sharing information.

The first thing the U.S. and the Soviet Union did, only months after the Cuban Missile Crisis, was set up a hotline, a 24-hour telecommunications link from Washington to Moscow. The idea was to give leaders a chance to communicate instantaneously to prevent accidental escalation.

That’s the kind of thing A.I. policy experts say could be adapted readily. Connecting not only Washington and Beijing but also the frontier labs would allow all sides to share information about worrying incidents. (In fact, my colleagues have reported that U.S. and Chinese officials have already discussed implementing such a system.)

Another is a nuclear-style inspection and monitoring regime. The International Atomic Energy Agency conducts intrusive in-person inspections of nuclear power plants in many countries to try to ensure nuclear material is used for peaceful purposes.

Instead of uranium enrichment, A.I. inspectors would monitor, say, caps on compute, the raw processing power that governs how powerful large language models are, said Anthony Aguirre, chief executive of the Future of Life Institute and an expert on A.I. safety and governance.

And A.I. might be a widely accessible tool, but the data centers that host it are as large-scale and specialized as enrichment facilities; satellites could help with monitoring them too.

In one respect, Aguirre said, it might even be easier to keep tabs on some A.I. The most advanced A.I. chips are, for now at least, typically manufactured by one Taiwanese company with machines produced by one Dutch company. In other words, they should be easy to trace. And they already have capabilities that can monitor A.I. computing power and be deactivated from afar if that compute is tampered with. “There’s already a kill switch, if we choose to use it,” Aguirre said. “But we need the political will.”

The Hiroshima factor

That’s of course where the rubber meets the road. China and the U.S. have major trust issues. Commitments that involve private companies, not just governments, add a complicating factor. And Beijing may balk at the idea of freezing A.I. development at a time when it’s still behind in the race. (The Soviets only agreed to cap their arsenal once they’d pulled even.)

Perhaps the biggest problem is that humans still don’t agree on the actual threat they’re facing.

That was not the case with nuclear weapons. Images of Hiroshima and Nagasaki are seared into our collective consciousness. The recent spate of rogue A.I. incidents has people concerned, but not at anything close to the same scale.

Still, alarm is growing. Aguirre’s institute organized the Pro-Human Assembly last week, a summit where a wide variety of people debated A.I. regulation. Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders appeared on the stage, one following the other, to demand tighter restrictions.

Bannon and Sanders are not exactly political allies, but the potential dangers of A.I. brought them together. It’s not the U.S. and China, but it’s a start.

item.title: At the U.N., Trump Lays Out a Winner-Takes-All Vision of U.S. Power
item.description:
The podium of the United Nations was an unusual setting for the leader of a global superpower to threaten to “annihilate the Islamic republic” of Iran or to declare that, in another conflict, “to the victor belong the spoils.”

Yet that was exactly what President Trump did on Tuesday, in threatening Iran if it failed to make a deal to end a war that had stretched far longer than Mr. Trump anticipated, and justifying his claims on Venezuelan oil reserves after American forces deposed its leader.

Mr. Trump has long made clear that he has little use for the United Nations, one of the post-World War II institutions that he has dismissed as outdated and ineffective. But his speech at the annual opening of the General Assembly amounted to a pure American rejection of the concept behind the U.N.’s founding in 1945: to “save succeeding generations from the scourge of war.”

The global body’s charter, written largely by the United States, expressly prohibited members from threatening or using force against a country’s territorial integrity unless acting in self-defense, or with the U.N.’s authorization.

On Iran, Mr. Trump made it clear that he, and he alone, would decide whether to strike a deal with Tehran’s leaders or “annihilate the Islamic republic.”

It may have been largely a negotiating tactic. A little later in the morning, American officials quietly met with Iranians who were also in New York for the opening session, though it was unclear whether any progress was made or whether Mr. Trump himself would meet top Iranian officials.

But his threats were not limited to the war that has consumed his presidency for months since the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran. He promised that Cuba’s government would fall, one way or the other. And if his “to the victor belong the spoils” line seemed drawn from the days of American gunboat diplomacy more than a century ago, that did not seem to bother the president. Mr. Trump has made it clear that he is willing to use the power of the U.S. military not only for the benefit of securing critical resources, like Venezuela’s huge oil reserves, but also to turn a profit.

Mr. Trump’s comments came at a moment when he appeared more isolated than ever from traditional allies, and when Americans were telling pollsters they overwhelmingly disapproved of his foreign policy. But none of that seemed to lead Mr. Trump to back away from the fiery threats that he has combined with military action in his second term.

Even by Mr. Trump’s standards, the speech seemed to disregard the foundational purpose of the U.N., an institution he has long derided as ineffective and unsuited to deal with the contemporary issues of the world.

It echoed a social media post earlier this year in which he threatened to wipe out Iranian civilization. But it was startling to hear such explicit threats from the podium of the United Nations. That seemed to be the president’s intent, as he celebrated taking actions that past presidents and the U.N. itself shied away from.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” Mr. Trump asked, before raising a far different prospect, with no apparent effort to differentiate between the country’s leadership and military and its civilians. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” Mr. Trump said from the General Assembly podium, where world leaders typically present themselves as champions of peace. He made no mention of his frustrations that a war he boasted would last only days or weeks had now stretched to just shy of seven months.

His speech, in short, seemed to embrace the core doctrine of his second term: that the United States would use a combination of overwhelming military and economic power to suit its own ends — and to bolster the national economy — rather than work through the painful, often slow diplomacy of deal-making and economic coercion. But he made no acknowledgment of the role of international bodies like the U.N., and seemed to suggest that they should simply line up behind the United States.

Later in the speech, he changed course, ticking off the list of conflicts he claimed he personally resolved, boasting that he saved millions of lives by intervening to prevent a war between Pakistan and India. And shortly after Mr. Trump threatened Iran with annihilation, his own aides met for three hours with Iranian officials. It was unclear what, if anything, was accomplished.

This celebration of power over principle built upon a belief that Mr. Trump talked about in an interview with The New York Times earlier this year, when he dismissed international law as a constraint on his actions. The only limit on his power, he said, was “my own morality, my own mind — it’s the only thing that can stop me.”

Venezuela was perhaps the most conspicuous example. He celebrated the swiftness with which Special Operations forces swept into Caracas, seized Nicolás Maduro and his wife from their bed, and delivered them to a detention center in Brooklyn, just a few miles from where Mr. Trump spoke.

Senator Andy Kim, Democrat of New Jersey, criticized Mr. Trump for promoting himself as both a president of peace and one that could wipe out a nation.

“Trump never misses a chance to humiliate himself in front of the world,” Mr. Kim said in a post on social media. “His war in Iran is a complete failure, and the American people are paying the price.”

And from the podium, other world leaders criticized Mr. Trump without mentioning his name. President Emmanuel Macron of France, a nation allied with the United States since the American Revolution, denounced a global retreat to the “law of the jungle.” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva of Brazil, the first world leader to speak on Tuesday, said that democracy was “once again under threat” and — without mentioning the U.S. operation against Mr. Maduro — insisted that the Venezuelan people had the right to self-determination. Mr. Trump has insisted that it is not the right time for an open election in the country.

Recent polling shows Americans are not on board with Mr. Trump’s approach. A CNN poll conducted last week showed that 29 percent of American adults approved of Mr. Trump’s handling of foreign affairs; 71 percent said they disapproved — reaching or exceeding levels of disapproval President George W. Bush faced in 2006, when the Iraq war was unraveling.

But to Mr. Trump, actions like seizing Venezuela’s leader and making claims on its oil were clear victories. “It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” he said. “If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States.”

Mr. Trump also described Cuba as a “failed state” that would soon fall. “We’ll not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep,” Mr. Trump said, prompting Cuban officials to walk out of the General Assembly.

“The US government proves incapable of accepting that #Cuba is, and has the right to be, a fully independent and sovereign country,” Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, Cuba’s foreign minister, later said on social media. “Cuba is not a threat to the US nor to any country.”

Mr. Trump also celebrated his administration’s recent deal on Greenland. Earlier this year he threatened a total takeover of the huge island, which is believed to have large underground reserves of rare-earth minerals used for making batteries, electric vehicles and other high-tech products.

Yet the prospect of the U.S. seizing a semiautonomous territory spurred intense backlash from European leaders and nearly upended the Western alliance.

After reaching a deal with Denmark and Greenland over the territory, Mr. Trump told the gathered crowd he planned to build two new military bases on Greenland — something the United States could have done in previous decades under an existing treaty.

Mr. Trump’s speech was also a pivot from his past remarks to the U.N., which were spent insulting world leaders and scolding them on their own policies. “Your countries are going to hell,” Mr. Trump said from the podium last year.

But now faced with a war in Iran with little sign of ending soon that has fueled discontent among his own supporters in the United States, Mr. Trump shifted from lecturing the international body to effectively selling them on his own actions — which have proved to be deeply unpopular with many Americans and allies overseas.

“I hope the Europeans realize that Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb,” Mr. Trump said in what amounted to a response to some of the world leaders that had criticized the war in Iran. “If they had succeeded, that wicked regime would have been free to spread terror and death forever.”

The declaration that Iran was building missiles that could reach Europe didn’t square with his earlier boasting of obliterating Iran’s nuclear program.

Mr. Trump claimed credit for ending the war in Gaza, even as humanitarian conditions there remain dire and a plan for disarming Hamas and withdrawing Israeli troops has been stalled for months.

Mr. Trump also attacked the International Criminal Court, which has issued an arrest warrant to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel over the war in Gaza, as a “rogue institution.”

The I.C.C. was established in a 1998 treaty to investigate and try people for war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity and the crime of aggression. The court cannot enforce its rulings and relies on its member states to detain people who are accused of crimes.

Mr. Trump called on all members of the International Criminal Court to resign immediately.

While the U.N. has said climate change is an existential threat and propelled the issue of artificial intelligence to the top of its agenda, Mr. Trump once again took a different approach. Climate change was nothing more than a “hoax,” Mr. Trump said.

And the United States rejected “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” artificial intelligence.

Mr. Trump did have one suggested change to the way the world approached A.I., one that made use of his penchant for branding.

“From this point forward, all of United States documents and hopefully the world’s will be changed to use the much more accurate term ‘super’ as opposed to ‘artificial,’” Mr. Trump said. “So it’s super intelligence.”

Mr. Trump then appealed for the leaders to refer to the rising technology as “S.I.” Whether they did, he said, would be a test of influence on the world stage — a question that has appeared to be consistently on the mind of the president.

“Let’s see if I have any power,” Mr. Trump said. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.”

item.title: As Trump Lobs Threats, Other World Leaders Mostly Avoid Talk of Iran
item.description:
Standing on a podium often reserved for messages of peace, President Trump on Tuesday brought his escalating threats against Iran directly before world leaders. They largely did not respond.

Mr. Trump told the United Nations General Assembly that he was deciding whether to “annihilate” Iran if the war — launched by the United States and Israel — drags on without a peace deal. But other world leaders said little about a conflict that has widely disrupted trade, driven up fuel prices and prompted Iranian attacks on other countries in the Middle East.

Those who did urged peace, not escalation.

Among them was Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, the emir of Qatar, which helped broker a June cease-fire between the United States and Iran that has fallen apart. He urged a return to negotiations to find a “lasting solution that ensures security and stability for the entire region, including Iran.”

“The opportunity for a peaceful diplomatic solution, which we believe is both possible and realistic, must not be missed,” he said.

The war has expanded to new fronts since Iran came under attack in February, with Iranian proxy forces repeatedly attacking military bases and ships across the region. Since the cease-fire between the United States and Iran broke down, there has been no clear off-ramp from the conflict.

The sides are locked in a showdown over the Strait of Hormuz that has suffocated global trade and led to sudden bursts of military activity.

As Mr. Trump’s ultimatum against Iran loomed over the gathering, the leaders of three countries affected by the conflict — Jordan, Qatar and Turkey, all U.S. allies — focused more on criticizing Israel over its conduct of the war in Gaza.

King Abdullah II of Jordan, caught in the middle as Iran strikes bases in his country used by the American military, did not criticize the United States for launching the war. But he did address its far-reaching consequences.

“If anyone had any doubt that conflict from our region stays there,” he said, “just look at the energy and grocery bills of ordinary families, from Mumbai to Minnesota.”

Sheikh Tamim, the Qatari emir, said the crisis was the result of “years of procrastination, managing crises with temporary fixes and unrealistic policies.” He said the region lacked safeguards for collective security.

Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said that he wanted an end to “the climate of war.”

“I strongly underline that any dangerous attempt to spread these conflicts, these clashes, to neighboring regions serves no one’s interests,” he said.

President João Lourenço of Angola, a country in southern Africa that is removed from the conflict geographically, said wars in other parts of the world had caused “instability on our continent,” with “devastating effects on the most vulnerable countries.”

“Today we live in an environment of global anarchy in which the use of force prevails over the force of reason and law,” he said.

President Gitanas Nauseda of Lithuania called attacks by Iranian-backed militant groups on neighboring countries a threat to international peace.

In his remarks to the General Assembly, the president of France, Emmanuel Macron urged the body to stand against those who want a world ruled by the “law of the jungle.” But he did not name those he believed responsible for fueling conflicts.

“The question before us, in very simple terms, is whether we want to live in this state of nature, with a kind of return to the law of the jungle, or in a civilized international society,” Mr. Macron said.

Iran was quick to reject Mr. Trump’s ultimatum as an empty threat. Iran’s armed forces, in a statement carried by state media on Tuesday, called his address an “exploitation of the U.N.’s podium to legitimize aggression, insecurity and global banditry.”

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is slated to speak to the assembly on Wednesday.

item.title: At U.N., Carney Lays Out a Broad Plan for a Divided World
item.description:
Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada expanded on his vision for international cooperation on Tuesday, outlining how nations can safeguard their mutual interests following a “rupture” to the world order by the United States and China.

“This is, in many respects, a time that comes once or twice every century,” Mr. Carney said during a news conference at the United Nations in New York, where he was attending the General Assembly. “What comes ahead, it’s not wishful multilateralism, which defends only the status quo, nor a cold realpolitik that dismantles the status quo altogether.”

He added: “The alternative that Canada and many others are pursuing, is values-based realism, an approach that’s both principled and pragmatic.”

In a highly publicized address to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland in January, Mr. Carney called on the world’s “middle powers” to band together to protect their interests from the decline of the “rules based order.” But he offered little detail what form that might take.

Until he was delayed by air traffic control disruptions on Monday, Mr. Carney had been scheduled to join leaders from the European Union and six other nations to launch an initiative he called “Partners for Multilateralism.”

“This is not a bloc or a bureaucracy,” he said in French on Tuesday. “It is a new forum that looks at universal institutions, practical coalitions and capacities that exist outside of governments in order to build trust and bring people together.”

He added: “The real choice is not between trying to preserve an international order established after the Second World War or abandoning it.”

He said that the plan acknowledges the impossibility of consensus among nations and suggested that alliances formed through the new group will be ad hoc and with changing memberships.

“Groups formed around problems rather than geography or size,” Mr. Carney said. “Not as an alternative to multilateralism, but as an instrument of it.”

Mr. Carney cited Canada’s work with France and Britain on a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, as well as Canada’s participation with other nations on preserving ocean environments as examples.

Such groups, Mr. Carney said, would bring their solutions to multilateral organizations, like the U.N., “to be strengthened, to be broadened and to be scaled.”

As he has suggested in the past, such a system demands that Canada and its traditional allies work pragmatically alongside nations with differing views.

“Put simply: we’re in a position where we need to pursue calibrated alliances, integrating deeply with those countries who share our values, remaining open-eyed with those who do not,” he said.

Mr. Carney’s remarks followed a similar message he delivered to the European Parliament where he called for a pact between Canada and the E.U. to help to secure sovereignty and independence for his country at a time of poor relations with the United States.

Mr. Carney will not address the U.N. General Assembly because of a scheduling conflict, but he is meeting with other leaders over several days in New York. Reflecting Mr. Carney’s rise on the world stage, he received more requests for meetings than his schedule could accommodate, said senior Canadian government officials.

Mr. Carney did not directly respond to questions about possibly meeting President Trump, saying: “I find that when you have 160 leaders come to New York that it’s most valuable to meet those who you don’t normally see.”

When asked about Mr. Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran, made in his address earlier on Tuesday, Mr. Carney replied in French: “There is a war underway, and he’s speaking the language of war.”

item.title: Outside the ‘Worried West,’ Many Feel Good About A.I.
item.description:
It may come as a surprise for world leaders discussing artificial intelligence at the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, but a large majority of people surveyed across the globe for a new Gallup poll said they felt mostly positive about A.I.

Gallup, an opinion research organization, interviewed at least 1,000 people in each of 37 countries and found that in 34, positive emotions toward A.I. outweighed negative feelings. An average of 72 percent of respondents said they felt curious, happy or excited about A.I., compared with 41 percent who felt worried, sad or angry.

It was among the most comprehensive portraits of varied emotional responses to the new technology yet, and the margins between hope and fear were wide.

In China and Vietnam, more than 90 percent of people polled said they believed that A.I. would mostly make daily life better. In Nigeria, Israel and Singapore, more than two-thirds of the respondents agreed.

But in the United States, only 36 percent saw A.I. as mostly helpful rather than harmful. The seven Western high-income countries that Gallup surveyed (the United States, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Canada, New Zealand, Malta and the Netherlands) dominated its ranking of the most concerned, with the United States at the top.

Gallup plans to eventually include A.I. surveys in 140 countries, but this early snapshot — conducted with Microsoft, featuring a margin of error of 2.2 percent and 4.9 percentage points — appeared to show a clear divide.

“The most consistent finding that is emerging is that these cluster of attitudes that we see in Western countries is pretty unique,” said Pablo Diego-Rosell, a senior scientist at Gallup. The “worried West,” he added, tends to feature high adoption, high concern and a belief that while A.I. might be good for the individual, it was less likely to be positive for their country.

Across 37 nations surveyed, the median percentage who have never tried A.I. is still relatively high — 57 percent. In the U.S., it’s 32 percent. But intense use is no predictor of dismay.

Some countries where survey respondents said they felt positively toward A.I. were also rapid adopters. Singapore, China and Israel all have a higher proportion of daily users than the United States. Others have lower rates of use: In Vietnam, only 12 percent of those surveyed use A.I. daily compared to 23 percent in the U.S.

Husan Chahal, an A.I. risk researcher for the National Bureau of Asian Research, said that many governments, especially in Asia, frequently framed the technology first and foremost as a tool for economic development, and were eager to drive A.I. uptake.

“That doesn’t necessarily mean they’re unconcerned about catastrophic risks,” she said. “But those risks may not be as prominent in their policy priorities.”

In almost every country polled by Gallup, the heaviest A.I. users said they were the least anxious about it. For example, 68 percent of daily A.I. users in the United States were worried about the technology compared with 80 percent of less frequent users, and 74 percent of those who had never used A.I.

Edward Lim, Vietnam country director for NUS Enterprise and BLOCK71, a start-up accelerator connected to the National University of Singapore, said that views of A.I. were evolving rapidly and in different directions.

He suggested that concerns were increasing in Singapore as the news of A.I. agents going rogue continued to spread, but in Vietnam, where human talent remains cost-competitive with A.I. agents, there is mostly excitement.

“What strikes me is how open people in Vietnam are to trying new things,” he said, adding, “The poll reflects what I see on the ground.”

item.title: It’s Not the Oscars: U.N. Speakers Love to Ignore Its 15-Minute Rule
item.description:
The United Nations has “kindly reminded” world leaders to keep their addresses this week to the General Assembly to 15 minutes. If history is any guide, many will be just as polite in ignoring the request.

Adhering to the clock is essential, the U.N. says, to schedule nearly 200 speakers over six days. It is also voluntary — a courtesy the organization acknowledges is rarely adhered to.

The chronic overrunning highlights a fundamental truth about the U.N.: It is a collection of sovereign states, and though it can cajole, it cannot force them to do anything.

“Part of being sovereign,” said David Bosco, an international relations expert at Indiana University Bloomington, “means no one gets to tell them when to shut up.”

When speakers surpass 15 minutes, there is no Oscars-style orchestra playing them off the stage or a cut to a commercial break. Delegates are informed that a light sits at the podium to assist with the “timely delivery” of speeches. They can ignore it, and historically they do.

Fidel Castro holds the General Assembly record for his four-and-a-half-hour address on Sept. 26, 1960. Wearing olive military fatigues, Mr. Castro lashed out at global capitalism, defended Cuba’s Soviet alliance and aired grievances about New York. (The overall U.N. record belongs to V.K. Krishna Menon, an Indian defense minister, who spoke for nearly eight hours across Security Council meetings in 1957 to defend India’s position on the disputed Kashmir territory.)

Most speakers on Tuesday, the first day of the General Assembly meeting, exceeded the allotted time. They included President Trump, who spoke for well over half an hour in an address in which he said he was weighing whether to strike a deal with Iran or “annihilate” it.

The General Assembly address is “essentially an ego trip for presidents and prime ministers,” said Richard Gowan, an analyst at the International Crisis Group. Once on the stage, “many of them cannot really hold back.”

Many speakers in fact aim their remarks at the audience back home, analysts said — a practical strategy, as speeches are often delivered to a largely empty hall. “Mostly they are just shouting into the void,” Mr. Gowan said.

A handful of leaders — including U.S. presidents and, more recently, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel — routinely command news media interest or prompt protest. But most statements fade quickly from memory.

The speeches that linger in U.N. lore are remembered less for their rhetoric than their theatrics.

In 1960, the Soviet premier, Nikita Khrushchev, banged (or maybe waved) his shoe from his desk in the hall in response to the speech by the Philippines’ delegate, who claimed the Soviet Union had deprived Eastern Europe of political and civil rights. In 1974, Yasir Arafat, chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization, addressed the session while wearing a gun holster. (A spokesman said Mr. Arafat did not carry a gun into the hall.)

In 2006, President Hugo Chávez of Venezuela draped a handkerchief over the timer light before declaring that the rostrum “smells of sulfur” after a speech the day before by President George W. Bush. Three years later, the Libyan leader, Col. Muammar el-Qaddafi, spoke for 100 minutes, tearing pages from a copy of the U.N. Charter. .

Paul Heinbecker, a former Canadian ambassador to the United Nations, relayed a diplomatic adage that he said could apply to just about any General Assembly session: “Everything had been said but not yet been said by everybody.”

item.title: Syria’s Leader, Though Strengthened, Faces Tests as He Addresses U.N.
item.description:
When President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria addressed the United Nations General Assembly last year, he was still in the throes of transforming his image from a rebel leader who once had ties to Al Qaeda into a head of state ushering in a new era in a country ruled for decades by dictatorship.

He returns to New York this year in a much stronger diplomatic position, and is scheduled to be the first speaker before the Assembly on Wednesday morning. Mr. al-Sharaa has secured significant sanctions relief, extended his government’s authority across most of Syria and gained international acceptance among a broad spectrum of foreign leaders, including President Trump.

Now, Mr. al-Sharaa now faces a more difficult test: turning those diplomatic ties into tangible gains for Syrians as mounting economic and security challenges threaten to undermine the country’s transition.

Syria’s economy remains in crisis and the flood of foreign investment his government hoped would quickly follow sanctions relief has not yet materialized. The World Food Program estimates that the monthly cost of essential needs for a family of five — including food, utilities and basic services — rose by almost 33 percent between June 2025 and June 2026.

The rising cost of living has deepened public frustration with Mr. al-Sharaa’s government. Last week, government increases in fuel prices triggered the country’s most widespread protests since Mr. al-Sharaa took power nearly two years ago, forcing his government to partially reverse the increases.

Mr. al-Sharaa is also struggling to restore Syria’s sovereignty in the face of Israel’s increasingly entrenched military presence in the south. Earlier this month, a U.N. commission investigating Syria reported that Israeli military operations in southern Syria had deepened, with repeated incursions, patrols, raids and searches disrupting civilian life. It warned that some Israeli actions, including the detention of Syrian civilians, could amount to war crimes.

Israel’s presence in southern Syria reflects its broader shift in defense strategy toward establishing military buffer zones beyond along its borders, including in southern Lebanon and Gaza. But its military activity in Syria is also bound up in a growing rivalry with Turkey, one of Mr. al-Sharaa’s closest allies and a longtime supporter of the rebel movement he once led.

Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the war in Gaza began in 2023. Turkey’s deepening military ties with Damascus have heightened Israeli concerns about the prospect of Turkish forces and equipment operating in Syria. Israel has struck Syrian military facilities that Turkey had assessed for possible use, underscoring the potential for Syria to become a flashpoint between the two regional powers.

Mr. al-Sharaa’s government has broken with its predecessors to express an openness to engage with Israel and has taken part in U.S.-mediated talks with Israeli officials in the hopes of easing tension. But that diplomacy has not yielded a security agreement or an Israeli withdrawal from southern Syria. And at a U.N. Security Council meeting last week, Syria’s permanent representative to the U.N., Ibrahim Olabi, also accused Israel of responding to Syria’s efforts at diplomatic engagement with “airstrikes, incursions and violations.”

“Israel penetrated our villages, displaced our people, bombed our facilities while we chose to spare the region further suffering,” Mr. Olabi said.

item.title: Myanmar Has an Envoy at the United Nations. Why Is He Not Speaking?
item.description:
All 193 member countries of the United Nations are entitled to address the General Assembly, but one was missing from the list of speakers this week. Where was Myanmar?

U Kyaw Moe Tun told The New York Times on Tuesday that he planned to be in Myanmar’s chair at the assembly hall in New York, his presence a quiet reminder of a civil war that the world has seemingly forgotten.

But he will not address the General Assembly, he said — in keeping with an arrangement that has allowed him to hold onto his post for the past five years, in open defiance of Myanmar’s military-backed government.

The elected government that sent Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun to New York in 2020 was ousted in a military coup the following year. Weeks after the putsch, he delivered a fiery speech to the General Assembly, pleading for international help to restore democracy to Myanmar. The junta announced his firing on state television the next day.

The United Nations still lists the ousted government — including Aung San Suu Kyi — as Myanmar’s official head of state. All along, the junta sought international legitimacy. This year, it has tried to transform itself into an elected government with elections that were widely seen as a sham.

The junta has written open letters to the U.N. secretary general António Guterres calling for Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun’s removal. Myanmar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement this month that Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun was living in the mission residence and using government funds without authorization.

Like other permanent representatives to the United Nations, Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun said he would spend the week preparing for the General Assembly’s six committees, in which countries discuss topics including disarmament, economic and social development, and humanitarian issues.

But his to-do list includes tasks from which most ambassadors are spared. He mows the lawn at his residence in upstate New York, drives himself to the United Nations building in the mission’s black Cadillac and finds his own parking in Manhattan.

Many of his staff have been let go to cut costs, Mr. Kyaw Moe Tun said in an interview last month. He stopped receiving a salary last year, he said, and the mission is running out of money.

item.title: The Secret History of Bats: A New Study Redraws Their Family Tree
item.description:
Bats are cryptic creatures. They inhabit the dark, roosting in hidden, often inaccessible places. And they possess some rare skills that can seem like superpowers: exceptional longevity, advanced echolocation abilities and a capacity for powered flight that is unique among mammals.

But their genes have been difficult to decipher and their fossils hard to find, leaving scientists puzzled about how these traits evolved — or even when and where bats first emerged.

A major new study — the largest analysis of bat genomes and fossils — sheds light on the origins of these mysterious mammals. The study, which was published on Wednesday in the journal Nature, suggests that the first bats emerged in Europe roughly 65 million years ago and that echolocation emerged early, before bats diversified into the many families existing today. It also presents a new evolutionary tree for bats, one that upends some previous conclusions about the relationships between different bat families.

The findings are “rewriting” the biological history of bats, said Ariadna Morales, an evolutionary biologist and research associate at the American Museum of Natural History and an author of the paper. “The evolutionary tree of bats changed.”

The study — which is the first phase of the Bat1K project, an effort to sequence and analyze the genomes of all living bat species — also lays the foundation for additional research into the underpinnings of their remarkable abilities.

“Bats are the most extraordinary of all our mammalian lineages,” said Emma Teeling, a zoologist at University College Dublin and a director of the Bat1K project, who is an author of the new paper. “This is a springboard.”

Bats are numerous, diverse and widely dispersed. There are roughly 1,500 living species of bats, which account for more than one-fifth of all mammal species, and they live on every continent but Antarctica.

For the study, scientists collected and sequenced the genomes of bats from 103 different species, spread across all 21 living families of bats. Then, they analyzed these genomes, and compared them with one another, using a variety of approaches. Some involved analyzing the full genomes of each species; others compared specific chromosomes, regions or other subsets of the data.

“Different parts of the genome tell different stories,” said Dr. Morales, an incoming assistant professor at the City University of New York.

But several lines of evidence converged, allowing the researchers to map the evolutionary relationships between different families of bats.

The resulting phylogenetic tree differed from previous ones in some notable ways. The sucker-footed bats of Madagascar, for instance, had been grouped with several bat families that live mostly in the neotropics. The new tree moved these Madagascar bats to the globally distributed superfamily that also contains vesper bats, the most common bats on the planet. The findings also suggested that this vesper bat superfamily was closely related to the superfamily containing sac-winged bats, whose members had previously been considered more distant relatives.

The researchers also analyzed bat fossils, using the data to estimate when different lineages had diverged and how bats spread across the globe.

Europe, Africa, North America and Asia had all been proposed as the birthplace of bats, but the new analysis pointed toward Europe. From there, bats most likely expanded into Africa and then to the rest of the globe, the researchers concluded.

The study also suggested that the fossil of an extinct echolocating bat belonged close to the base of the evolutionary tree — and that echolocation appeared before the modern lineage of bats did.

Scientists have long debated whether echolocation or flight evolved first in bats. One influential study, based on a 52-million-year-old fossil and published in 2008, suggested that flight evolved first.

But the new analysis, which is based on a much larger data set, indicates that the question is far from settled.

“It looks pretty clear that echolocation evolved before the diversification of all the living families,” said Nancy Simmons, a curator emerita at the American Museum of Natural History who is an author of the new paper, as well as the 2008 one.

“Now we’re sort of back where we were a number of years ago, which is flight and echolocation seem to have evolved at the base of the tree,” she added. “And we still don’t know whether they came at the same time, or one came before the other.”

The researchers said that they hoped that their new evolutionary tree would be a resource for scientists studying the genes and genetic variants that underpin flight, echolocation, disease resistance and more. That work is already underway at Bat1K, Dr. Teeling said.

“To be able to uncover evolutionary history is extraordinary,” she said. “But there’s so much more we can do with this.”

item.title: Walkouts Are a Longstanding Tradition at the U.N. General Assembly
item.description:
Nearly 200 world leaders get a lectern and two microphones to make their point at the United Nations General Assembly. The 1,000 or so lower-ranking diplomats in the hall have to settle for more limited options for self-expression: Stay seated or leave.

Walking out has become something of a tradition in recent years. On Wednesday, the lone U.S. diplomat in the hall left his seat as President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran accused the United States of targeting his country’s civilians. It was a mirror image of the day before, when the Iranian delegations’ seats were nearly empty as President Trump described the choice he said he faced with Iran: make a peace deal or “annihilate” the country.

The Cuban delegation also exercised its right to leave the hall on Wednesday. As Mr. Trump labeled the country a “failed state” and vowed to bring about the downfall of its government, four Cubans stood up and walked briskly to the exit.

Rosa Freedman, a professor of law at the University of Reading in England who specializes in the United Nations, said walkouts were a permitted form of diplomatic protest that U.N. delegates had practiced for decades. “So long as it’s done peacefully, then there are no rules that prevent states from walking in and out,” she said.

For over 70 years, walk out they have. During the throes of Algeria’s war for independence from France throughout the 1950s, French diplomats left the hall when the body raised the conflict — something Paris held was none of the U.N.’s concern. In 1956, Hungary’s delegation walked out of the General Assembly after the Soviet invasion of Budapest. When South Africa’s foreign minister defended his country’s system of racial apartheid in a speech during the 1964 session, diplomats from about 40 countries staged a walkout.

When President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad of Iran repeated incendiary conspiracy theories in 2010, suggesting that the United States had orchestrated the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, delegates from over 30 countries walked out, including the American diplomats.

Last year, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel delivered his address before a sea of empty chairs, as many diplomats refused to take their seats in protest of Israel’s war in Gaza. Once Mr. Netanyahu started speaking, the number of diplomats who walked out was so high that they had to form a line to reach the exit.

Conducted peacefully, Professor Freedman said, walkouts are an important expression of freedom of speech and assembly, hallmarks of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted soon after the body’s founding. She also noted that in comparison to parliamentary chambers, the General Assembly can be hectic.

“People are constantly walking in and out of the rooms and walking around the rooms, sometimes on mobile phones,” she said. “The filing out from the room in protest does not have the same level disruption as it would do in a parliamentary body, where everyone keeps their seat for the duration of a session.”

item.title: Zelensky Is Expected to Warn Russia’s Aggression Won’t Stop at Ukraine’s Borders
item.description:
When President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine addressed the United Nations General Assembly for the first time after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, his appeal for international support was fueled by raw moral indignation.

Mass graves in the newly liberated Ukrainian city of Izium had just been uncovered, and the atrocities in Bucha and other reclaimed towns continued to shock the international community. “A crime has been committed against Ukraine, and we demand just punishment,” he declared in a prerecorded video address.

When Mr. Zelensky takes the stage on Wednesday, he will no longer be pleading merely to awaken the world to the war’s horrors, but also demanding the means for his nation to survive and warning that the violence will not remain confined to Ukraine.

On Tuesday, he met with President Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York and said that he hoped Russia’s war in his country would end “before winter” and that the Trump administration would help Kyiv do it.

“I think we need to do this as quick as possible — before winter,” Mr. Zelensky said. Mr. Trump nodded and repeated his words with approval.

Mr. Zelensky’s speech will most likely revisit core themes from his previous addresses, including global food security, the urgent need for advanced air defenses, and warnings about the proliferation of artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons systems in warfare.

“We are now living through the most destructive arms race in human history,” he told the General Assembly last year.

The early consequences of that race are already clear. Escalating destructive capabilities on both sides can been seen in brutal frontline combat that kills or wounds thousands of soldiers every month and in relentless long-range bombardment campaigns.

Mr. Zelensky is also expected to reinforce his consistent message that Russia’s aggression will not stop at Ukraine’s borders.

Moscow is already testing how far it can push abroad, analysts say, strangling global grain routes to pressure the developing world while waging a brazen campaign of arson, sabotage, and cyberattacks across Europe.

Mr. Zelensky has frequently argued that Russia and its key partners — North Korea and Iran — seek to dismantle the American-led security architecture established after World War II and are the primary agents of chaos in a world beset by crises.

His diplomacy faces added complexity, however, given Mr. Trump’s disdain for the traditional alliances that served as the backbone of global stability.

Mr. Zelensky must navigate a delicate political line: invoking what were once the foundational values of American foreign policy without alienating an administration pursuing an approach starkly different from its predecessors.

As America has pulled back from its traditional role, European democracies have struggled to fill the void.

Mr. Zelensky is expected to argue once more that securing the continent requires defeating Russian forces in Ukraine and degrading Moscow’s capacity to wage war.

Four years after the invasion, civilian casualties from Russian strikes have surged. through a relentless daily toll: a family killed when a missile hit its home at midnight; two people killed in a drone strike at a gas station; five dead after a public bus is struck.

As Ukraine prepares for what may be the most challenging winter of the war, Mr. Zelensky must convey the critical urgency of his nation’s plight to world leaders increasingly distracted by competing global crises and domestic political pressures.

item.title: Stanislas Hutin, Who Denounced Torture in France’s Algerian War, Dies at 95
item.description:
Stanislas Hutin, whose firsthand account of witnessing torture by French troops in the Algerian war of independence helped incite a wave of revulsion against that losing conflict, died on Sept. 2 in Arradon, in Brittany, France. He was 95.

His death was announced by Ouest-France, a large-circulation daily newspaper that Mr. Hutin’s father founded after World War II.

Mr. Hutin’s testimony — published anonymously in June 1956 and soon republished by well-known French antiwar writers — was among the earliest to chronicle the systematic torture practiced by French forces against Algerians attempting to free themselves from colonial rule, and it was among the most influential.

Mr. Hutin was a 24-year-old Jesuit seminarian when he was conscripted in 1955. His army unit, the 21st Colonial Infantry regiment, was sent as part of a “pacification” effort — he used the phrase derisively in a 2019 interview — deep into the Algerian countryside.

He was a most reluctant recruit, as he made clear in the interview, conducted by the historian Tramor Quemeneur for the national audiovisual archive. Mr. Hutin, a machine-gunner, said, “I wrote a text before I left” France, “pleading with the Lord that this machine wouldn’t spit death because of me.”

After disembarking from his troop transport, he was shocked by the poverty of the Algerians and the brutality that his officers displayed toward them. Beatings of suspects were the order of the day, but much worse was to come.

How The Times decides who gets an obituary. There is no formula, scoring system or checklist in determining the news value of a life. We investigate, research and ask around before settling on our subjects. If you know of someone who might be a candidate for a Times obituary, please suggest it here.

He was preparing to go to sleep in his tent, in a French encampment in Algeria’s northeast, on a cold night in late January 1956, when he was startled out of his bed.

“The cries of a pig being slaughtered I heard last night around 9 p.m. came, indeed, from the young boy,” he began his journal entry for the next day. The boy was a shepherd of 14 whom the French soldiers had captured two days earlier.

“At first I thought it was the jackals,” he wrote in the little red spiral-bound notebook he kept, clandestinely. “But it kept going on and on.”

“So I got out of the tent in my pajamas and listened: voices and groans were coming from the lieutenants’ tent. I said to myself: ‘They can’t possibly be subjecting that kid to the magneto.’ ” (That was the name of the troops’ portable field generator, which had often been put to sinister use: Wires from it were attached to various parts of a victim’s body, notably the testicles. And it left no detectable trace of torture.)

“I went back inside, once more broken and sickened,” he wrote.

“It was the boy,” he continued. “This morning, I’m literally shattered.”

Already considered a “Communist” by the officers in his unit, “I really got into it” with the lieutenant who had done the torturing, he told Mr. Quemeneur years later. “A brute, a sadist,” he wrote in his journal the next day.

He took a picture of the teenager, Said Boutout, “to show to people in France” the face of the French army’s brutality: a curly-haired boy so youthful he barely looked 14.

The photo of the teenage Said, who survived the ordeal, later appeared on book covers. “It became, for me, a real memorial of this abominable war,” Mr. Hutin told Mr. Quemeneur.

Mr. Hutin was back in France by the spring of 1956, and that June, a Jesuit priest published excerpts from Mr. Hutin’s journal in the order’s publication L’Action Populaire.

The following year, as opposition to the Algerian war was growing, extended portions appeared in a short collection of testimonials, “Des Rappelés Témoignent” (“Recruits Testify”), published by a group of Christian intellectuals.

Also in 1957, Pierre-Henri Simon, a Catholic writer who became Le Monde’s literary critic, published “Contre la Torture” (“Against Torture,” not translated), including extracts from Mr. Hutin’s journal. It was a book that “marked an entire generation,” the Catholic journalist Jean-Claude Petit wrote when it was republished in 1999. And the eminent classical historian and antiwar activist Pierre Vidal-Naquet cited him extensively in his book “La Torture dans la République” (1972).

For Mr. Hutin, the small red notebook and the letters he had written to his family, served a private, not just public, purpose. “My family, journalists, when I came back, they wanted to know,” he told Mr. Quemeneur. “It allowed me to liberate myself from this traumatism. It was a real catharsis.”

Stanislas Hutin was born in Rennes, France, on Sept. 7, 1930, the third of five sons of Paul Hutin-Desgrées, a journalist, World War I veteran and leading figure in the Mouvement Républicain Populaire, the Christian-democratic party that became a force in post-World War II politics. His mother was Magdeleine Desgrées du Loû.

Journalism ran in the family: Mr. Hutin’s maternal grandfather had founded the newspaper L’Ouest-Éclair at the end of the 19th century, the ancestor of Ouest-France.

Mr. Hutin’s father was imprisoned by the Germans in 1943. “We were continually confronted by the occupying forces,” Mr. Hutin recalled in the 2019 interview. Friends in the Resistance were shot by the Germans, a memory that shaped his reaction in Algeria later.

In 1951, he entered the Jesuit order and three years later was drafted to serve in Madagascar, another African colony that France was vainly trying to hold on to. On his return, he helped compose a report exposing slavery on a Madagascar coffee plantation. The report gained some attention because his father was by then a member of the French Parliament.

Sent to Algeria in the summer of 1955, he was designated for service as a teacher by the French army, as part of the “pacification” campaign. He recalled in the 2019 interview that “the captain ordered me to keep a rifle next to the blackboard, a flagrant contradiction.”

He left the Jesuits after the war — it ended in 1962 with France’s humiliating defeat — studied sociology and ethnology, and pursued a career aiding commercial development and banking in developing countries, especially Africa.

He is survived by a brother, Gonzague Hutin.

In the late 1970s through ’80s, when he returned to Algeria as a development worker, Mr. Hutin sought out Mr. Boutout, the teenager who had been captured and abused. They ended up establishing a rapport, Mr. Quemeneur said.

In his retirement, he spoke frequently in French schools about the lessons of the Algerian misadventure. “He was someone of great humanism,” Mr. Quemeneur said of Mr. Hutin. “He was open to others, and open to dialogue. He accepted the positions of others. And he dedicated his life to the service of others.”

item.title: 6-Year-Old Girl in China Sets a Rubik’s Cube Record
item.description:
Lian Yunzhi grabbed an ordinary Rubik’s Cube and solved it in under five seconds. Then she did it four more times.

Her average time was a new women’s world record.

Lian Yunzhi is 6 years old.

In video of a Rubik’s Cube competition in Wuhan, China, held on Sept. 13, Yunzhi, wearing a headband with a red bow, picks up the 3x3x3 cube, spins it with blinding speed, then drops it onto a table, fully solved.

After some attempts, she looks up implacably. But when she pops a particularly good time — under 4 seconds in one case — she breaks into a smile and claps her hands.

Yunzhi’s average time for five solves, dropping the fastest and slowest, was 4.52 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which governs competitions and tracks record times for mechanical puzzles like Rubik’s Cubes. Three days later in Guangzhou, she lowered the record to 4.27 seconds.

The men’s record is 3.51 seconds, and is held by Yiheng Wang, who is 12.

Speed cubers, as competitive Rubik’s Cube solvers are known, study patterns and learn move combinations that will help them solve more quickly. But at the elite level, the key is “Don’t think, just solve,” Max Park, an American speed cuber, told The New York Times.

Cube records were once largely held by teenagers and people in their early 20s. In recent years, however, preteens have started taking over the top spots.

Many are from China, which has schools that teach speedy Rubik’s Cube solving.

Cube enthusiasts also explain the plummeting age of champions by pointing to kids’ enthusiasm for the puzzle, their ability to learn quickly and that they simply have more time to practice. Yunzhi practices two to three hours a day, her mother told Red Star News of Chengdu, China, via Agence France-Presse.

There are records for other, more challenging cubes as well. The women’s record for the more complex 4x4x4 cube is 23 seconds and change. Too easy? Then learn to solve a 7x7x7 and try to break the record of 1:49.

Oh, and the Rubik’s Cube has also been solved in under 20 seconds blindfolded.

item.title: At the U.N., Japan’s Leader Says It’s Time to End ‘Enemy State’ Label
item.description:
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called on the United Nations on Tuesday to scrap references to former Axis powers as “enemy states” in its Charter — a World War II-era designation that China and Russia have recently used to attack Tokyo.

Ms. Takaichi, in her first appearance before the United Nations General Assembly in New York, described Japan as a “peace-loving nation” and said the references “must be deleted.”

“I would like to strongly emphasize this position as Japan has the pride and honor of its significant contributions to the efforts of the United Nations over the last 70 years,” she said.

The U.N. Charter, drafted during the final months of World War II, includes several references to “enemy states.” At the time, the Allies wanted to preserve a way to act against the re-emergence of militarism or fascism among Axis powers like Japan, Germany and Italy, without having to consult the newly formed U.N. Security Council.

Japan’s leaders have called the “enemy state” label anachronistic. In 2005 the U.N. General Assembly passed a resolution in support of removing the language. But it has been difficult to get the backing of the U.N. Security Council; any of its five permanent members, including Russia and China, can veto any measure. Some are concerned that removing the language could open the door to other revisions, such as changing the makeup of the Security Council, that would dilute their influence.

China has seized on the “enemy states” term recently to attack Japan, part of a monthslong effort to punish the country over comments Ms. Takaichi made about Taiwan. In November, Ms. Takaichi said that Japan could intervene militarily if China were to attack Taiwan, a self-governed democracy that Beijing considers part of its territory.

Beijing has since accused Tokyo of reviving World War II-era militarism, pointing to Ms. Takaichi’s efforts to rebuild the military. After Ms. Takaichi’s remark last year, the Chinese Embassy in Japan said the “enemy state” clause permitted the use of force against former Axis powers if they adopted a “policy of aggression.”

Russia has also invoked the term. Last month, its foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, told reporters in Moscow that Japan was designated an “enemy state” in the U.N. Charter. He was answering a question about a territorial dispute between Russia and Japan.

Jeff Kingston, a professor of modern Japanese politics and history at Temple University’s Tokyo campus, said Ms. Takaichi wanted to remind the United States “whose side Japan has been on for the past eight decades as a model international citizen.” She was also trying to “draw a line in the sand” with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, and Russia’s leader, Vladimir V. Putin.

“She is playing to an international audience and seeking to highlight how this outdated clause is politicized by Japan’s adversaries,” he said.

Ms. Takaichi had a full agenda in New York, where she met with President Trump on Tuesday, a day before he was set to host Mr. Xi for a state visit in Washington.

Ms. Takaichi had been eager to meet Mr. Trump before the visit to brief him on China’s increasingly aggressive economic and military measures against Japan, and to highlight Japan’s investments in the American economy.

Seated next to Mr. Trump at U.N. headquarters, Ms. Takaichi said the meeting demonstrated “the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance to the world.”

Mr. Trump praised Ms. Takaichi, saying, “She’s going to go down as one of the great prime ministers.”

Ms. Takaichi had faced pressure at home to question Mr. Trump about his administration’s recent decision to impose sanctions on the president of the International Criminal Court, Tomoko Akane, a Japanese judge. The decision has stirred deep anger in Japan, and Ms. Takaichi has called it “very unfortunate.”

Ms. Takaichi said at a news conference in New York on Tuesday that she had raised the issue, though she did not provide details, according to NHK, Japan’s public broadcaster.

Ms. Takaichi used her appearance at the U.N. to promote her country’s desire to play a more active global role in defense and economic matters.

She issued a stark warning about the changing world order, saying the “stable post-Cold War era is now a thing of the past.” She pitched her country as a force for stability and strength, ready to help on issues like artificial intelligence, climate change and nuclear disarmament.

“Japan feels a sense of responsibility to safeguard the ideals of the United Nations as our beacon of hope,” she said. Ms. Takaichi, a defense hawk, did not mention China by name, though she criticized Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

She also expressed an openness to dialogue with North Korea, after recent calls by South Korea to ease sanctions on Pyongyang.

At the U.N., Ms. Takaichi also raised a longstanding concern for Japan: the fate of 17 citizens that Japan says North Korea abducted decades ago. North Korea has acknowledged only that its agents abducted 13 Japanese people in the 1970s and ’80s. Five of them returned to Japan in 2002. North Korea has said the others died long ago.

item.title: Youth Frustration and Migration Shadow Morocco’s Election
item.description:
Migration and the frustrations of young people hang over Wednesday’s elections in Morocco.

In the last year, young people have been at the center of two major national crises: the 2025 Gen Z protests and the sudden, deadly mass crossing this summer into Ceuta, a sliver of the European Union on Morocco’s northern coast.

The issues that drove those crises are at the forefront of the legislative elections: unemployment is high, schools and hospitals are crumbling, and the space for public expression is shrinking.

King Mohammed VI and the country’s government are betting that co-hosting the 2030 soccer World Cup, along with Spain and Portugal, will inject investment and vigor into the country’s economy and offer some distraction from popular disenchantment.

Morocco is a constitutional monarchy in North Africa, where 27 parties are on the ballot with candidates competing for 395 seats in the lower house of the Parliament.

Two centrist parties, the National Rally of Independents, and the Authenticity and Modernity Party, are the front-runners, according to an analysis published by the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis.

The two parties, part of the governing coalition since 2021, have made jobs and the economy the central theme of their campaigns. The National Rally of Independents includes Rachid Talbi Alami, the current speaker of Parliament.

One of the most visible political figures is Fouzi Lekjaa, the budget minister and president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, who joined the Authenticity and Modernity Party in July. The party, which is seen as being particularly close to the monarchy, hopes to capitalize on his track record in delivering projects related to the World Cup, said Riccardo Fabiani, who heads the North Africa Project of the International Crisis Group, a nongovernmental organization.

Morocco’s young people have had an ambivalent relationship with electoral politics and the World Cup.

People aged 18 to 24 make up 12 percent of the population but just 4 percent of registered voters.

In October last year, thousands of young people protested the deaths of eight women at a dilapidated hospital in Agadir, a city on the Atlantic coast. Their slogans contrasted the millions that the government was spending on the World Cup with the dire state of public services.

The protests, inspired by similar youth movements in Nepal and Madagascar, began after a loosely organized group known as Gen Z 212 demanded that Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch step down.

Instead, the government responded with a crackdown that left at least three people dead and produced hundreds of arrests. In the wake of the protests, the space for public expression shrank even more, with the arrests of popular musicians and artists who critiqued the government.

“Despite the Gen Z protests, Morocco is not going back on prioritizing the World Cup,” Mr. Fabiani said. “This is seen by the monarchy as a strategic investment in the future development of the country.”

The protests “clearly exposed the extent of the gap between some young people and political institutions,” said Mohamed Al Ghafri, a Moroccan human-rights activist. There is, he added, “an accumulated sense that political participation is futile.”

Morocco’s economy grew by a fairly robust 4.9 percent last year, driven in part by World Cup spending, according to figures from the World Bank.

But unemployment is high — 13 percent last year — and about one-third of young Moroccans are jobless. About one-fifth of the work force is considered underemployed, in jobs that do not match their qualifications.

“This campaign is fought almost entirely on economic ground: jobs, unemployment, health, education and purchasing power,” said Rachid Aourraz, co-founder of the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis. “Parties and voters now care more about the cost of living than political questions.”

While headlines trumpet lower inflation, consumer prices remain high after a increases over several years, according to figures from the International Monetary Fund. Energy prices are expected to drive inflation up again this year, the I.M.F. predicts.

Successive years of drought and extreme weather have added further strain.

While parties have made promises to fix the broad issues driving migration, few address it head-on.

At least 141 people died, most of them Moroccans who drowned trying to swim to Ceuta, a Spanish territory, in the summer’s sudden exodus of young people trying to cross the border.

The surge caused a political crisis in Spain, but Moroccan politicians have largely avoided talking about it. No party has raised any questions about accountability or demanded an inquiry into the deaths, said Myriam Cherti, a researcher at the Center on Migration, Policy and Society at the University of Oxford.

“It has become kind of an emotional reference point of the campaign without producing direct or distinct policy debates around migration,” Ms. Cherti said.

Remittances from émigrés are an important part of Morocco’s economy, representing for many people the possibility of a more promising life abroad.

“Migration is the emotion of the campaign, but never directly part of its substance,” Ms. Cherti said.

item.title: U.S. Rebukes Australia Over Proposed Limits on Social Media Algorithms
item.description:
The United States has admonished Australia over a proposed new law that would allow social media users in the country to opt out of algorithms used to decide what content they can see on platforms like Facebook, Instagram and TikTok.

In a statement, the U.S. Embassy in Canberra said on Tuesday that the proposed changes could amount to censorship by limiting the reach of content generated by Americans and restricting the business activities of American companies.

“If Australia compels platforms to aggressively filter content in algorithmic feeds to satisfy a government mandate, and such filtering draws in protected speech,” the embassy wrote, “the effect on a disfavored speaker or media source’s reach would not be meaningfully different than outright removal.”

“The U.S. government would likely consider such a measure as facilitating censorship,” said the statement, which called on Australia to withdraw plans that “suppress content based on ambiguous government-defined safety criteria.”

Australia has already placed controls on technology firms by becoming the first country in the world to introduce a nationwide ban on children younger than 16 having access to social media accounts.

The right to opt out of social media algorithms was announced earlier this month as part of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s proposed Digital Duty of Care law, which aims to give users more control over the content they see online. Platforms would be required to notify users that they can decide whether to include content recommended by algorithms in their social media feeds. Companies that failed to comply could face large fines.

“It’s not about giving government control, it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices,” Mr. Albanese said in response to the U.S. Embassy’s criticism.

He added he would always stand up for Australia’s national interests. (Mr. Albanese later posted a selfie with President Trump, saying they had spoken on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.)

Dali Kaafar, a professor at Macquarie University and executive director of its Cyber Security Hub, said that it was unusual for the United States to intervene so directly in a matter of domestic Australian law, particularly using “language this strong.”

“These platforms operate globally, but the algorithms governing what Australians see, what is amplified to them and how their attention is shaped are largely designed and controlled overseas,” Professor Kaafar said. “Australia has a legitimate interest in deciding what protections and choices should apply to people using those systems in Australia.”

Most users are unlikely to opt out of content recommended by algorithms because the customized content is the reason they are spending more time on the apps, said Tama Leaver, a professor of internet studies at Curtin University in Perth.

“It is strange for the administration to take such a strong position on this when the likelihood is that even if it was implemented, it wouldn’t do much damage to the company’s bottom line,” Professor Leaver said, referring to the Trump administration.

The proposed changes also would not affect the freedom of speech for anyone inside the United States, he added, though “it might impact their reach in a fairly minimal sense.”

Social media companies already comply with local laws in other countries such as Germany, which bans use of Nazi symbols, he said.

The proposed Digital Duty of Care law will also require companies to limit harmful content, such as that promoting self-harm or eating disorders, on their A.I. chatbots, online games and apps and to limit addictive design features.

The U.S. Embassy issued its objections as world leaders convened at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, where artificial intelligence was at the top of the agenda.

A.I. companies have acknowledged that their agents have gone rogue and hacked into corporate systems, prompting calls for more guardrails around the rapidly developing technology. However, Mr. Trump has said he would reject “any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” artificial intelligence.

Victoria Kim contributed reporting.
